Test 5
What’s the purpose of gaining knowledge?

A
‘I would found an institution where any person can find instruction in any subject.’ That was the founder’s motto for Cornell University, and it seems an apt characterization of the different university, also in the USA, where I currently teach philosophy. A student can prepare for a career in resort management, engineering, interior design, accounting, music, law enforcement, you name it. But what would the founders of these two institutions have thought of a course called ‘Arson for Profit’? I kid you not: we have it on the books. Any undergraduates who have met the academic requirements can sign up for the course in our program in ‘fire science’.

B
Naturally, the course is intended for prospective arson investigators, who can learn all the tricks of the trade for detecting whether a fire was deliberately set, discovering who did it, and establishing a chain of evidence for effective prosecution in a court of law. But wouldn’t this also be the perfect course for prospective arsonists to sign up for? My point is not to criticize academic programs in fire science: they are highly welcome as part of the increasing professionalization of this and many other occupations. However, it’s not unknown for a firefighter to torch a building. This example suggests how dishonest and illegal behavior, with the help of higher education, can creep into every aspect of public and business life.

C
I realized this anew when I was invited to speak before a class in marketing, which is another of our degree programs. The regular instructor is a colleague who appreciates the kind of ethical perspective I can bring as a philosopher. There are endless ways I could have approached this assignment, but I took my cue from the title of the course: ‘Principles of Marketing’. It made me think to ask the students, ‘Is marketing principled?’ After all, a subject matter can have principles in the sense of being codified, having rules, as with football or chess, without being principled in the sense of being ethical. Many of the students immediately assumed that the answer to my question about marketing principles was obvious: no. Just look at the ways in which everything under the sun has been marketed; obviously it need not be done in a principled (=ethical) fashion.

D
Is that obvious? I made the suggestion, which may sound downright crazy in light of the evidence, that perhaps marketing is by definition principled. My inspiration for this judgement is the philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that any body of knowledge consists of an end (or purpose) and a means.

24

Reading
E
Let us apply both the terms ‘means’ and ‘end’ to marketing. The students have signed up for a course in order to learn how to market effectively. But to what end? There seem to be two main attitudes toward that question. One is that the answer is obvious: the purpose of marketing is to sell things and to make money. The other attitude is that the purpose of marketing is irrelevant: Each person comes to the program and course with his or her own plans, and these need not even concern the acquisition of marketing expertise as such. My proposal, which I believe would also be Kant’s, is that neither of these attitudes captures the significance of the end to the means for marketing. A field of knowledge or a professional endeavor is defined by both the means and the end; hence both deserve scrutiny. Students need to study both how to achieve X, and also what X is.

F
It is at this point that ‘Arson for Profit’ becomes supremely relevant. That course is presumably all about means: how to detect and prosecute criminal activity. It is therefore assumed that the end is good in an ethical sense. When I ask fire science students to articulate the end, or purpose, of their field, they eventually generalize to something like, ‘The safety and welfare of society,’ which seems right. As we have seen, someone could use the very same knowledge of means to achieve a much less noble end, such as personal profit via destructive, dangerous, reckless activity. But we would not call that firefighting. We have a separate word for it: arson. Similarly, if you employed the ‘principles of marketing’ in an unprincipled way, you would not be doing marketing. We have another term for it: fraud. Kant gives the example of a doctor and a poisoner, who use the identical knowledge to achieve their divergent ends. We would say that one is practicing medicine, the other, murder.

25

questions.instruction: Choose the correct heading for each section from the list of headings below.
options: i Courses that require a high level of commitment
ii A course title with two meanings
iii The equal importance of two key issues
iv Applying a theory in an unexpected context
v The financial benefits of studying
vi A surprising course title
vii Different names for different outcomes
viii The possibility of attracting the wrong kind of student
questions.evidence: The writer asks what the founders would have thought of a course called ‘Arson for Profit’ and adds, ‘I kid you not’. The paragraph’s focus is the shock value of the course title.
questions.distractorAnalysis: ii is tempting because the title can later be read in two ways, but Section A only presents it as startling. vi captures the paragraph as a whole; i and v are unsupported, and the remaining headings belong to later sections.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct heading for each section from the list of headings below.

viii The possibility of attracting the wrong kind of student
questions.evidence: The course is intended for arson investigators, but the writer asks whether it would also be perfect for prospective arsonists.
questions.distractorAnalysis: vi describes the first reaction to the title in Section A. Section B moves to the risk that the same specialist knowledge could attract or assist the wrong students, so viii is the precise match.

questions.instruction: Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
questions.prompt: This is a university course intended for students who are undergraduates and who are studying 33 __________.
questions.translation: 这是一门大学课程，面向正在学习 ______ 的本科生。
questions.evidence: Any undergraduates who have met the academic requirements can sign up for the course in our program in ‘fire science’.
questions.distractorAnalysis: ‘Arson for Profit’ is the course title, not the subject program the undergraduates are studying. ‘fire science’ supplies the required noun phrase and uses exactly two words.

questions.instruction: Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
questions.prompt: The expectation is that they will become 34 __________ specialising in arson.
questions.translation: 人们预计他们将成为专门从事纵火案件的 ______。
questions.evidence: Naturally, the course is intended for prospective arson investigators.
questions.distractorAnalysis: The summary already adds ‘specialising in arson’, so ‘arson investigators’ would be repetitive though within the limit. The official key requires the head noun ‘investigators’.

questions.instruction: Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
questions.prompt: The course will help them to detect cases of arson and find 35 __________ of criminal intent.
questions.translation: 课程将帮助他们发现纵火案件，并找到犯罪意图的 ______。
questions.evidence: Students learn to establish a chain of evidence after detecting whether a fire was deliberately set and discovering who did it.
questions.distractorAnalysis: ‘chain of evidence’ is three words and exceeds the limit; the one-word official answer ‘evidence’ fits both the grammar after ‘find’ and the meaning.

questions.instruction: Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
questions.prompt: … leading to successful 36 __________ in the courts.
questions.evidence: The chain of evidence is established ‘for effective prosecution in a court of law’.
questions.distractorAnalysis: ‘court of law’ names the venue, but the blank requires the legal outcome after ‘successful’. ‘prosecution’ is the exact noun from the passage and the official key.

questions.instruction: Decide whether the statement agrees with the views of the writer: YES, NO, or NOT GIVEN.
questions.prompt: It is difficult to attract students onto courses that do not focus on a career.
questions.translation: 很难吸引学生参加不以职业为导向的课程。
options: YES
NO
NOT GIVEN
questions.evidence: The writer says students can prepare for many careers, but never states whether non-career courses have difficulty attracting students.
questions.location: Section A, sentence 3; no statement elsewhere resolves the claim
questions.distractorAnalysis: Career-focused examples do not logically prove recruitment difficulty for other courses. There is neither agreement nor contradiction, so NOT GIVEN.

questions.instruction: Decide whether the statement agrees with the views of the writer: YES, NO, or NOT GIVEN.
questions.prompt: The ‘Arson for Profit’ course would be useful for people intending to set fire to buildings.
questions.translation: 纵火牟利课程会对打算纵火烧楼的人有用。
options: YES
NO
NOT GIVEN
questions.evidence: The writer asks rhetorically whether this would be ‘the perfect course for prospective arsonists to sign up for’.
questions.distractorAnalysis: Although the writer disapproves ethically, the statement concerns usefulness, not approval. The rhetorical question affirms that the knowledge could help arsonists, so YES.

questions.instruction: Decide whether the statement agrees with the views of the writer: YES, NO, or NOT GIVEN.
questions.prompt: Fire science courses are too academic to help people to be good at the job of firefighting.
questions.translation: 消防科学课程过于学术化，无法帮助人们做好消防工作。
options: YES
NO
NOT GIVEN
questions.evidence: The writer explicitly says the academic programs ‘are highly welcome’ as part of increasing professionalization.
questions.distractorAnalysis: The later warning about a firefighter torching a building concerns misuse of knowledge, not excessive academic content. ‘highly welcome’ contradicts the statement, so NO.

questions.instruction: Decide whether the statement agrees with the views of the writer: YES, NO, or NOT GIVEN.
questions.prompt: The writer’s fire science students provided a detailed definition of the purpose of their studies.
questions.translation: 作者的消防科学学生对其学习目的给出了详细定义。
options: YES
NO
NOT GIVEN
questions.evidence: The students ‘eventually generalize to something like, “The safety and welfare of society”’, which is broad rather than detailed.
questions.distractorAnalysis: The students do provide an answer, but ‘generalize’ and ‘something like’ directly undermine the claim that it was detailed. Therefore the statement contradicts the passage.
